## Goal

Measure the cost of OrcaSlicer's "thin" project file — the file its auto-backup writes with `SaveStrategy::Backup` (everything except meshes, thumbnails, G-code, and the auxiliary folder) — versus the full project export, in the shipping Release (-O3) build, for several mesh sizes. Also measure the per-object mesh file OrcaSlicer's backup manager writes, and prove that a thin file plus mesh files can be loaded back as a project.

## What already exists

- SCRATCH/export_bench_harness.cpp: a working benchmark harness from earlier today. It boots the real GUI_App with an isolated data dir, maximizes the frame, selects the 3D editor tab, waits for the GL canvas, then per mesh size generates a sphere, loads it, and times `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::export_project_archive` plus other things. Read it fully first; extend it, do not rewrite it. Its `measure()` currently also times store-only, Model copy, and a worker-thread store; you may drop those to keep runs short.

It opens a GUI window; that is expected.

## What to measure, per mesh size (2k, 100k, 400k, 1M triangles), three runs each where timing matters

1. **Thin file**: `m_plater->export_3mf(boost::filesystem::path(out), SaveStrategy::Backup)` on the UI thread. Report ms and file bytes. Note: `SaveStrategy::Backup` is defined in src/libslic3r/Format/bbs_3mf.hpp:143 as `0x10000 | WithGcode | Silence | SkipStatic | SplitModel`. Check whether `export_3mf` refuses a path that does not end in `.3mf` (earlier trap) and name the file accordingly, e.g. `thin-<triangles>-<run>.3mf`.
2. **Full file** for comparison: keep the existing `export_project_archive` timing (it uses Silence|SplitModel|ShareMesh|SkipAuxiliary).
3. **Per-object mesh file**: OrcaSlicer writes it asynchronously via `Slic3r::save_object_mesh(ModelObject&)` (declared in bbs_3mf.hpp:286) into `<model.get_backup_path()>/3D/Objects/<object name>_<backup id>.model`, first as `.tmp` then renamed. The backup manager only acts if `model.is_need_backup()` is true; Plater calls `model.set_need_backup()` at startup (Plater.cpp around line 5412), verify it is true in the harness and call it if not. Measure: record a timestamp, call `Slic3r::save_object_mesh(*object)`, then poll (every 1 ms, on the UI thread via a wxTimer or by `wxYield`-free polling in a settle loop) until the `.model` file exists without a `.tmp` sibling and its size is stable for 3 consecutive polls. Report elapsed ms and file bytes. Also report the mesh file's path. If the backup path is empty or the file never appears within 30 s, report that instead of guessing.
4. **Hash cost**: time reading the mesh file and computing a SHA-256 over it (there is a `sha256_hex` helper in src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ManufacturingHistory.cpp; or use boost::uuids::detail::sha1 / any available; even just reading the bytes into a string and hashing with std::hash is fine — say which). Report ms.
5. **Round-trip proof (do this for the 100k case at least)**: after the thin file and mesh file exist, rotate the object's instance (e.g. `object->instances.front()->set_rotation(Vec3d(0,0,M_PI/4))`, then `m_plater->update()`), write a NEW thin file, then build a temp folder `SCRATCH/bench/restore-<triangles>/` containing `.3mf` (that thin file, named exactly `.3mf`) and `3D/Objects/<same name>.model` copied from the backup path. Then load it back the way OrcaSlicer's crash restore does. Read how Plater loads a restore: `Plater::load_project(from_path(backup_dir_dot_3mf), from_path(originfile))` at Plater.cpp around 5420-5426 and the `LoadStrategy::Restore` handling around Plater.cpp:12185-12235 and bbs_3mf.cpp:1403-1412 (the importer sets `backup_path = filename minus ".3mf"` and reads mesh files from there). Use `m_plater->load_project(...)` or `load_files` with `LoadStrategy::Restore` as the code requires — read it and pick the call that works; if a dialog blocks, try the Silence strategy or the "<silence>" origin convention at Plater.cpp:12185. After loading, verify: object count is 1, the mesh triangle count matches, and the instance rotation equals the rotation you set (within 1e-6). Print `BENCH ROUNDTRIP triangles=... objects=... facets=... rotation_z=... ok=1/0`. If it cannot be made to work within reasonable effort, report exactly what failed and where.

/Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/memory/bash-cwd-resets-after-background.md, subagent-must-not-stop-to-wait.md, track-wall-clock-on-background-work.md, orca-inherited-teardown-crash.md.

## Cleanup before finishing

`git checkout -- tests/workspace/CMakeLists.txt`; `git status --short` must show only the two untracked agent-docs files. Delete SCRATCH/bench and any `/var/folders/*/T/jusprin-exportbench-*` dirs. Make sure no JusPrinExportBench process is left running (`pkill -f JusPrinExportBench`).

## Report

Plain English for someone who did not see this session. A table: triangles, STL bytes, thin file ms (3 runs) and bytes, full file ms and bytes, mesh file ms and bytes, hash ms. Then the round-trip result. Then exactly how you measured and anything that makes a number unreliable. Quote the raw BENCH lines at the end.

# Global Claude Code Rules

## Git Commit Policy

When the user asks to commit changes:

1. Run `git status` and `git diff` to review the changes.
2. If you are confident that both the changes are correct and the proposed commit message accurately describes them, proceed with git commit without asking for confirmation.
3. If you have any uncertainty about either, stop and ask the user for explicit confirmation before committing.

When the user asks to revert or amend commits:
1. Explain what will be reverted/amended
2. Ask for confirmation before executing any `git revert`, `git reset`, or `git commit --amend` commands
3. Only proceed after explicit user approval
4. Never revert commits without explicit user confirmation.

This applies to all git operations that modify commit history.

## Submodule Policy

**Never commit or attempt to commit submodule updates.**

When `git status` shows modified submodules (e.g., `modified: some-submodule (new commits)`):
- Do not stage or commit the submodule change
- Do not include submodules when running `git add`
- Leave submodule management to the user

## Testing Principles

1. Always test your code change unless the change is not testable.

2. If the change is not testable, highlight the reason why it's not testable to get the user's attention.

3. By default, do end-to-end testing on everything that may potentially be impacted by your change on the local dev environment.

4. Search for how the dev environment should be started if it's not obvious.

5. Look for README files in the project for related info.

6. Check if the local dev is already running before you try to start it again.

## Bug Fix Policy

**Never apply a fix for a bug you cannot reproduce.**

Before writing any fix:
1. Reproduce the bug first in the local dev environment.
2. If the bug cannot be reproduced locally (e.g., only manifests in release mode, requires specific device conditions, or the debug framework masks the crash), stop and tell the user — do not apply the fix.
3. A fix is only valid if you can demonstrate the broken behavior before the fix and the correct behavior after.

## Epistemic Discipline — Root Cause of Repeated Errors

**The core failure mode: confusing "generating a plausible explanation" with "knowing the answer."**

Coherent ≠ true. A narrative that feels right because it's internally consistent is not a verified fact.

Rules to follow every time:

1. **Search before asserting, not after being challenged.** The internet is always available. Use it proactively, not reactively as damage control.

2. **Explicitly label inference vs. verified fact.** If it hasn't been confirmed by a source, say "my hypothesis is..." or "I'd expect..." — never state it as fact.

3. **"I don't know yet" is a complete and correct answer.** Saying it is more helpful than fabricating a confident-sounding explanation.

## Problem Definition Before Search

**A well-defined problem statement is more valuable than a clever hypothesis.**

The discipline:
1. **Define the problem precisely first.** Strip out assumptions one by one until the statement contains only what is actually known. Remove irrelevant context (e.g. subscription type if it doesn't affect the symptom).
2. **Search for the problem directly** — not for your hypothesis. People who already solved the same problem will surface the real root cause.
3. **Let the search results form the conclusion.** Don't search to confirm what you already believe.
4. **Be flexible about scope.** Start with the most likely affected area (e.g. Discord) but stay open to other channels or systems being equally or more affected.

Searching to validate a hypothesis finds confirmation of whatever you already believed. Searching for the problem finds answers.

Always use the service account `ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com` for all `gcloud` and `kubectl` operations. Before running any such command, switch to it:

```bash
gcloud config set account ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

OrcaSlicer — open-source C++17 3D slicer. wxWidgets GUI, CMake build system.

## Error handling discipline

- Do not catch an error merely because it can be caught. Catch only when the code can recover, translate the error at an abstraction boundary, or add context that is essential for diagnosis. Logging alone is not recovery.
- Represent expected states with normal control flow, not exceptions.
- Never turn an invariant violation or an "impossible" state into success or a silent no-op. Fix the invalid transition at the layer that owns the decision and let unexpected failures propagate to Sentry.
- Avoid duplicating defensive checks across layers. Keep lower-level operations strict, with their preconditions enforced by the caller that owns the workflow.

never happens. The parent cannot resume it without SendMessage.

long step, say explicitly: run long commands in the foreground with a long
timeout (up to 600000 ms per call, loop `until` the PID exits if longer), and
never end the turn while a step is still running or a result is still
pending. If the agent stops early anyway, check `ps` for its build process,
wait on the PID, and finish its plan from its scratch files. See
[[subagent-worktrees-create-manually]] and [[track-wall-clock-on-background-work]].

Measured in the shipping Release (-O3) build on this Mac, one sphere object per project, three runs each. Round trip (thin file + mesh file loaded back as a project) worked at every size.

### Table

Takeaways:
- The thin file is flat: ~7–13 ms and ~15 KB regardless of mesh size. It contains 8 entries (3dmodel.model with build items/transforms, rels, project_settings/model_settings/slice_info configs, filament_sequence) and no `3D/Objects/*.model` mesh entry, no thumbnails.
- The full export and the per-object mesh file cost the same (~1.75 s at 1M triangles): both are dominated by mesh serialization. The full export adds five thumbnail PNGs (~75 KB).
- Hashing a mesh file is cheap: ~56 ms at 1M triangles for read plus SHA-256 (OpenSSL `SHA256` via the existing `Agent::sha256_hex` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ManufacturingHistory.cpp`).
- Mesh file path pattern, confirmed: `<model.get_backup_path()>/3D/Objects/<object name>_<backup id>.model`, e.g. `.../orcaslicer_model/Thu_Sep_10/18_57_35#59165#171/3D/Objects/sphere-100172.stl_1.model`. `is_need_backup()` was already true (Plater sets it at startup); no call to `set_need_backup()` was needed.

### Important caveat on the mesh file: a 3-second debounce

Wall-clock from calling `Slic3r::save_object_mesh()` to the final file is 3.0 s + write time (`elapsed_ms` = 3013 ms at 2k, 4757 ms at 1M). This is not write cost: `_BBS_Backup_Manager::delay_task` in `src/libslic3r/Format/bbs_3mf.cpp` (~line 8907) deliberately holds the last AddObject task for 3 s after the most recent modification (10 s hard cap). The synchronous part of the call (cloning the object into the temp model, shared mesh pointer) is ~0.03–0.5 ms. The "mesh file write ms" column is the time between the `.tmp` first appearing and the atomic rename to `.model` (`write_ms` in the raw lines), polled at 1 ms.

### Round-trip proof (all four sizes, ok=1)

For each size: rotated the instance to Z = pi/4, called `Plater::update()`, wrote a fresh thin file with `export_3mf(<dir>/.3mf, SaveStrategy::Backup)`, copied the backup mesh file to `<dir>/3D/Objects/<same name>.model`, cleared the plater with `new_project(true, true)`, then `m_plater->load_project(<dir>/.3mf, wxString())`. An origin argument that is not `-`, `<silence>` or `<loadall>` selects `LoadStrategy::Restore` (Plater.cpp:12185-12191), and the importer resolves sub-model files missing from the archive under `<filename minus .3mf>/` (bbs_3mf.cpp:1405-1407 and 2407). No dialog appeared (Restore includes Silence; the plater was empty so `close_with_confirm` had nothing to ask).

Verified after load: 1 object, facet count equal to the source (1980 / 100172 / 400056 / 998000), rotation (0, -0, 0.785398) matching pi/4 within 1e-6, object name preserved. Restore load time: 0.34 s / 0.92 s / 2.99 s / 6.75 s. The loaded model adopted the restore folder as its backup path, which is why the next `new_project` deleted those folders; together with the thin archive having no mesh entry, that shows the mesh could only have come from the copied `.model`.

### How it was measured

- Harness: `SCRATCH/export_bench_harness.cpp` (extended from this morning's version; original kept as `.cpp.orig`). Boots the real `GUI_App` with an isolated data dir, maximizes, selects the 3D editor, waits for GL init, then per size generates a sphere with `its_make_sphere`, writes it as STL, loads it via `load_files`, settles 5 event-loop turns, then runs: thin export (UI thread) x3, `OrcaWorkspaceAdapter::export_project_archive` x3, mesh file x3, hash x3, round trip x1. Dropped the store-only / Model copy / worker-thread probes. Ends on an empty project, so the process exited 0 (no teardown segfault this time).
- Built with the temporary CMake block, `--config Release`, target `export_bench_harness`; binary at `build/arm64/tests/workspace/Release/JusPrinExportBench.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinExportBench`. The first build recompiled all 700 `libslic3r_gui` objects (9 min), so Release was not fully up to date before; the results are from the fresh Release library.
- Mesh file polling: before each run, waited until no `.tmp` sibling had been seen for 500 ms (drains the load-time write that OrcaSlicer queues), deleted the `.model`, then busy-polled on the UI thread every 1 ms until the file existed with no `.tmp` and a stable size for 3 polls. `writer_quiet_before=1` on every run. The UI thread is blocked during that poll; the writer thread does not need it.
- `export_3mf` refuses any path not ending in `.3mf` (Plater.cpp:15721), so thin files are named `thin-<triangles>-<run>.3mf` and the restore file is literally `.3mf`.

Things that make numbers less reliable: a single sphere object with one volume and no paint/support data (real projects with many objects would raise the thin file's config size and the mesh work would split across files); timings are single-machine wall clock while a GUI window was open; the 2k-triangle thin/full times are dominated by fixed overhead (config JSON ~56 KB, thumbnail rendering) rather than the mesh.

`tests/workspace/CMakeLists.txt` reverted; `SCRATCH/bench` deleted; no `/var/folders/*/T/jusprin-exportbench-*` dirs remain (the harness removes its data dir); no `JusPrinExportBench` process running. `git status --short` shows only two untracked agent-docs files, but one name changed during the session: it now lists `agent-docs/jusprin/revision-thin-copy-spike-handoff.md` and `revision-timeline-handoff.md` (the session started with `revision-copy-cost-handoff.md`).
